segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: Ed, how are you getting on with the reading for our presentation next week?

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: Well, OK, Ruth – but there’s so much of it.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: I know, I hadn’t realised birth order was such a popular area of research.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: But the stuff on birth order and personality is mostly unreliable. From what I’ve been reading a lot of claims about how your position in the family determines certain personality traits are just stereotypes, with no robust evidence to support them.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: OK, but that’s an interesting point – we could start by outlining what previous research has shown. There are studies going back over a hundred years.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: Yeah – so we could just run through some of the typical traits. Like the consensus seems to be that oldest children are generally less well-adjusted because they never get over the arrival of a younger sibling.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: Right, but on a positive note, some studies claimed that they were thought to be good a nurturing – certainly in the past when people had large families they would have been expected to look after the younger ones.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: There isn’t such a clear picture for middle children – but one trait that a lot of the studies mention is that they are easier to get on with than older or younger siblings.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: Generally eager to please and helpful – although that’s certainly not accurate as far as my family goes – my middle brother was a nightmare – always causing fights and envious of whatever I had.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: As I said – none of this seems to relate to my own experience. I’m the youngest in my family and I don’t recognise myself in any of the studies I’ve read about. I’m supposed to have been a sociable and confident child who made friends easily – but I was actually terribly shy.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: Really? That’s funny. There have been hundreds of studies on twins but mostly about nurture versus nature...

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: There was one on personality, which said that a twin is likely to be quite shy in social situations because they always have their twin around to depend on for support.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: My cousins were like that when they were small – they were only interested in each other and found it hard to engage with other kids. They’re fine now though.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: Only children have had a really bad press – a lot of studies have branded them as loners who think the world revolves around them because they’ve never had to fight for their parents’ attention.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: That does seem a bit harsh. One category I hadn’t considered before was children with much older siblings – a couple of studies mentioned that these children grow up more quickly and are expected to do basic things for themselves – like getting dressed.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: I can see how that might be true – although I expect they’re sometimes the exact opposite – playing the baby role and clamouring for special treatment. ——————————–

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: What was the problem with most of these studies, do you think?

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: I think it was because in a lot of cases data was collected from only one sibling per family, who rated him or herself and his or her siblings at the same time.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: Mmm. Some of the old research into the relationship between birth order and academic achievement has been proved to be accurate though. Performances in intelligence tests decline slightly from the eldest child to his or her younger siblings. This has been proved in lots of recent studies.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: Yes. Although what many of them didn’t take into consideration was family size. The more siblings there are, the likelier the family is to have a low socioeconomic status – which can also account for differences between siblings in academic performance.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: The oldest boy might be given more opportunities than his younger sisters, for example.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: Exactly.

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: But the main reason for the marginally higher academic performance of oldest children is quite surprising, I think. It’s not only that they benefit intellectually from extra attention at a young age – which is what I would have expected. It’s that they benefit from being teachers for their younger siblings, by verbalising processes.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: Right, and this gives them status and confidence, which again contribute, in a small way, to better performance. So would you say sibling rivalry has been a useful thing for you?

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: I think so – my younger brother was incredibly annoying and we fought a lot but I think this has made me a stronger person. I know how to defend myself ( / ). We had some terrible arguments and I would have died rather than apologise to him – but we had to put up with each other ( / ) and most of the time we co-existed amicably enough.

segments.speaker: ED
segments.en: Yes, my situation was pretty similar. But I don’t think having two older brothers made me any less selfish – I was never prepared to let me brothers use any of my stuff ...

segments.speaker: RUTH
segments.en: That’s perfectly normal, whereas ...
